title: Relationship with Goodman; Maxwell, Bernstein, Gil Evans
summary: He got along with Benny; talk of Jimmy Maxwell, Artie Bernstein and Gil Evans.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: What kind of a relationship did you have with Benny?
A very good one. I always got along with Benny. He had his quirks but you accept those things, everyone does.
In one way or another.
He might have been parsimonious, sometimes thoughtless, but I can accept that.
What about some of the other people on the band? You mentioned--
Jimmy Maxwell?
That's a good start; yeah.
Jimmy, in those days, I considered a good friend of mine. He married a girl who was the sister of Benny's bass player at the time.
Artie Bernstein?

Artie Bernstein. He came to Benny's band from Sacramento. I guess he'd been in Gil Evans' band. I think that's who it was before that. Gil used to have a band in (inaudible) Beach, I remember going down there with Red Norvo
in '38 when he had one there.
What did it sound like? Is that a dumb question?
That's not a dumb question, but I don't know that I can answer it. It was good.
Did it sound like anything that, for example, he wrote later for Claude Barnhill (phonetic spelling), or I won't try to go beyond that?
I can't answer that, I don't know.

But Jimmy, when he came with Benny, was very taken with eastern cultures He used to sleep on a straw mat, lived on bananas and studied Japanes; he used to talk Japanese. This was in 1940, just before the war. He was always a unique human being and turned out to be a very good trumpet player.
Still is.
I know.
He's still a good lead player too. He's gotten more chances I think in recent years to be a soloist, a great plunger player.
Good musician.
No question.
